name: Herding Behavior
description: When people can see what others chose, they may copy the crowd instead of relying on their own information. A few early visible choices can snowball into a self-reinforcing adoption pattern.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to trending lists, review counts, popularity sorting, marketplaces, app stores, recommendation feeds, and any interface that makes prior choices highly visible to later users.
myth_risk_note: Herding behavior is well-established in economic theory and financial markets with strong empirical documentation, but the theoretical models are more thoroughly validated than field measurement of the behavior's real-world prevalence.
prevalence_note: Common in growth, marketplace, and social-product discussions about popularity cues and trend amplification, though the neighboring 'social proof' label is more mainstream in broad UX practice.

findings.description: An informational cascade occurs when it becomes optimal for an individual to imitate the observed behavior of predecessors and disregard their own private information, even when following the crowd may be wrong; this mechanism explains why localized conformity to a fad, fashion, or custom can arise and also why such mass behaviors can be fragile — small new information can abruptly reverse a cascade.
findings.source_title: A Theory of Fads, Fashion, Custom, and Cultural Change as Informational Cascades

findings.description: In a sequential decision model where each individual can observe the choices of those who decided earlier, it is rational for later individuals to imitate predecessors' choices rather than act on their own private information, producing herd behavior at the population level; the resulting equilibrium is informationally inefficient (early, possibly-wrong choices can cascade through the whole population).
findings.source_title: A Simple Model of Herd Behavior

applications.title: GameStop, January 2021: a 2,700% intraday price swing driven by visible crowd momentum, per the SEC's own report
applications.description: The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission's own October 14, 2021 staff report on the January 2021 'meme stock' episode documents GameStop (GME) stock rising approximately 2,700% intraday between its January 8 low and January 28 high, before falling more than 86% within about a week. The report ties the run-up directly to visible social dynamics rather than independent fundamental analysis: heavy discussion and short-squeeze speculation on the Reddit forum WallStreetBets, a documented single-day 23.93% price jump when Chewy co-founder Ryan Cohen's investment was disclosed, and a further acceleration once his board appointment was announced -- with average daily share volume rising over 1,400% and broker-dealer app downloads (Robinhood, Webull) surging in parallel. The report itself is explicit that many participants' stated reasons for buying (an anticipated 'short squeeze' against short-selling professional investors) were as much about the visible crowd and its stated intent as about any independent analysis of GameStop's own fundamentals.
applications.industry_context: Retail equities trading; the phenomenon spanned social media (Reddit) and mobile trading apps (Robinhood, Webull) at once, not one single platform.
applications.ethical_note: This wasn't a company or designer deliberately engineering herding behavior in users -- it was an emergent, largely voluntary crowd phenomenon among retail investors themselves, which the SEC's own report explicitly declines to fully explain ('the underlying causes... are a subject of speculation that is beyond the scope of this report'). Real financial harm landed on investors who entered late in the cycle, but whether any party's design or promotion crossed from organizing enthusiasm into genuine manipulation is a real, unresolved question this source itself doesn't settle -- graded unclear rather than forcing a verdict the evidence doesn't support.
